scope: Original core flashcards in the first school mocks, 20 Physics AS + 20 taught Chemistry + 20 Maths Year 1 Pure; excludes Chemistry buffers and Maths Year 2
purpose: Correct exact-ID legacy card answer calibration, each with one further sound correct paraphrase and one explicit common misconception. Preserve existing model, prompt, original variants and learner progress ID.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What happens in particle–antiparticle annihilation?
records.back: Their rest mass/energy is converted to photons while energy and momentum are conserved.
accept: A particle and its antiparticle annihilate to produce photons, conserving energy and momentum.
reject: Annihilation converts all energy into a single photon without needing to conserve momentum.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is a couple, and what is the moment of a couple?
records.back: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with separated lines of action. Resultant force = 0. Moment of the couple = Fd, where d is the perpendicular separation.
accept: A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces acting at different lines of action; net force is zero and moment is one force times perpendicular separation.
reject: A couple is a single force whose moment equals force multiplied by time.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why do electron-diffraction rings shrink at higher accelerating voltage?
records.back: Momentum rises, so de Broglie wavelength and diffraction angle fall.
accept: Greater accelerating potential increases electron momentum, reducing de Broglie wavelength and the scattering angle.
reject: Increasing the accelerating voltage makes the electron wavelength longer and diffraction rings wider.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How is atomic excitation different from the photoelectric effect?
records.back: Excitation moves an electron to a higher bound energy level. The photoelectric effect removes an electron from the metal.
accept: Atomic excitation raises an electron within bound levels whereas photoelectric emission ejects an electron from a surface.
reject: Excitation and the photoelectric effect both simply raise the electron to a higher bound level.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What common forces might appear on a free-body diagram?
records.back: Weight acts vertically down; normal contact force acts perpendicular to a surface; tension acts along a string; drag/friction acts opposite relative motion or its tendency.
accept: Include weight vertically down, normal force perpendicular to contact, tension along a cord, and friction opposing relative movement.
reject: The normal reaction points vertically down on any slope and friction always acts uphill.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A projectile is launched horizontally. What changes if the launch height doubles while speed stays constant?
records.back: Time of fall and horizontal range both increase by a factor of √2 (assuming no air resistance).
accept: Both the fall time and the horizontal range scale by the square root of two if the launch height is doubled.
reject: Doubling the height doubles the flight time for a horizontal launch.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from a 45 m cliff. Find its range (g=10 m s⁻²).
records.back: 45 = ½(10)t² ⇒ t=3 s. Range = horizontal speed × time = 15×3 = 45 m.
accept: t = sqrt(2h/g) = 3 seconds and horizontal range = 15 times 3 = 45 metres.
reject: The range is 15 m because the horizontal launch speed never changes.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: State Newton's third law and explain why the two forces do not cancel.
records.back: Interacting objects exert equal, opposite forces of the same type on each other, acting on different objects, so they do not cancel on one object.
accept: The third-law pair has equal and opposite forces on different bodies, so they do not cancel on one body.
reject: Action and reaction cancel because both forces act on the same object.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A force pulls a block at angle α above an inclined plane. How does this affect R?
records.back: The outward pull reduces R: if there are no other normal forces, R = mg cosθ − F sinα.
accept: The force has an outward perpendicular component F sin alpha, so R = mg cos theta - F sin alpha.
reject: The outward pulling force makes the normal reaction increase by F sin alpha.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How does Newton's second law differ from the third law?
records.back: Second: net force on ONE object changes its momentum. Third: forces pair across TWO interacting objects.
accept: Newton II describes the effect of resultant force on one body; Newton III pairs forces on two different bodies.
reject: Newton's second and third laws both refer to two forces that act on the same body.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How can graph-axis units identify whether an area is impulse or work?
records.back: Force×time gives N s (impulse); force×displacement gives N m or J (work).
accept: Area of F against time has units N s and is impulse; area of F against distance has units N m or joules and is work.
reject: An area of force against time is work measured in joules.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does zero gradient on a displacement–time graph show?
records.back: Zero velocity: stationary at that instant or throughout a flat segment.
accept: A zero displacement-time gradient means instantaneous velocity is zero.
reject: A zero displacement-time slope shows constant nonzero speed.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A straight sloping v–t line crosses zero. What changes?
records.back: Direction changes if velocity changes sign; speed falls to zero then rises.
accept: When the velocity crosses zero and reverses sign the body changes direction, with speed first dropping to zero.
reject: Crossing v=0 on a velocity-time graph means acceleration has become zero.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: For curved s–t graphs, how is instantaneous velocity found?
records.back: Find the gradient of the tangent at that time.
accept: Draw a tangent at the chosen point of the curved displacement-time plot and calculate its slope.
reject: Find instantaneous velocity by taking the total area under the displacement-time graph.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How do you identify acceleration on a v–t graph?
records.back: Gradient Δv/Δt; a horizontal line means zero acceleration.
accept: Acceleration is the slope of velocity versus time, so a flat section corresponds to zero acceleration.
reject: The area under the velocity-time graph always gives the acceleration.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: On a 30° slope, which component of weight pulls downhill?
records.back: mg sin30°; the perpendicular component is mg cos30°.
accept: Weight downhill component is mg sin(30 degrees), with mg cos(30 degrees) normal to the plane.
reject: The component of weight downhill on a 30 degree slope is mg cos 30 degrees.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A horizontal push up a slope does what to the reaction?
records.back: It adds a component into the surface, increasing the normal reaction.
accept: A horizontal force up the incline has an inward normal component, so it raises the reaction.
reject: A horizontal push uphill always reduces the normal contact reaction.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the moment of two equal opposite forces forming a couple?
records.back: One force × perpendicular separation of their lines of action.
accept: The couple moment is Fd, using the perpendicular distance between the two force lines.
reject: The moment of a couple is Fd/2 using the full separation d.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does the gradient of a displacement vs t² graph give in free fall?
records.back: g/2, for release from rest with negligible drag.
accept: For release from rest s=(1/2)gt squared, so the slope of s against t squared is g/2.
reject: The slope of displacement against time squared is always g, even starting from rest.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Acceleration stays at +3.0 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. Find the velocity change.
records.back: Signed area under a–t = 3.0×4.0 = +12 m s⁻¹.
accept: Delta v is +3.0 times 4.0, which equals +12 m/s.
reject: The change in velocity is 0.75 m/s.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is entropy, qualitatively?
records.back: A measure of disorder of a system, related to the possible arrangements of particles and energy.
accept: Entropy describes the spread or dispersal of energy among possible arrangements, often approximated as disorder.
reject: Entropy is simply the total heat released by a reaction.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why is a proton-transfer step often shown at the end?
records.back: To obtain the neutral product after an O- or N-containing nucleophile adds.
accept: A final proton transfer can remove the extra hydrogen and leave a neutral ester or amide product.
reject: The final proton transfer is always needed to create a carbon-carbon double bond.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the organic product class of acyl chloride hydrolysis?
records.back: A carboxylic acid.
accept: Hydrolysing an acyl chloride yields a carboxylic acid.
reject: Hydrolysing an acyl chloride directly gives a primary amide.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the organic product class of alcohol acylation?
records.back: An ester.
accept: Acylating an alcohol yields an ester.
reject: Acylation of an alcohol yields an alkene as the main organic product.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the organic product class when ammonia is acylated?
records.back: A primary amide, RCONH₂.
accept: Acyl chloride plus ammonia gives an unsubstituted primary amide, RCONH2.
reject: Ammonia acylation gives an N,N-disubstituted amide.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the organic product class when a primary amine is acylated?
records.back: An N-substituted amide, RCONHR′.
accept: An acyl chloride and primary amine form an N-substituted amide.
reject: A primary amine reacts with an acyl chloride to make an alcohol.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Which by-product distinguishes acyl chlorides from acid anhydrides?
records.back: Acyl chlorides give HCl; anhydrides give a carboxylic acid.
accept: Acyl chloride reactions make HCl, while corresponding acid anhydrides produce a carboxylic acid as by-product.
reject: Acyl chlorides produce ethanoic acid as by-product and anhydrides produce HCl.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the main organic product of acid anhydride hydrolysis?
records.back: Carboxylic acids.
accept: Acid anhydride hydrolysis gives carboxylic acids.
reject: Hydrolysing an acid anhydride forms a ketone and oxygen gas.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What main organic product classes arise from anhydride alcoholysis?
records.back: An ester and a carboxylic acid.
accept: An acid anhydride and an alcohol form an ester together with a carboxylic acid.
reject: Anhydride alcoholysis produces an ester and hydrogen chloride.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What type of amide forms from anhydride and ammonia?
records.back: A primary amide.
accept: The product class is a primary amide, RCONH2.
reject: Anhydride and ammonia produce a tertiary amide.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What type of amide forms from anhydride and a primary amine?
records.back: An N-substituted amide.
accept: Acylation of a primary amine by an anhydride yields an N-substituted amide.
reject: Acid anhydride and primary amine chiefly give an ester.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What does the N- prefix mean in the name N-methylethanamide?
records.back: A methyl substituent is bonded to the amide nitrogen.
accept: N-methyl means methyl is attached directly to the nitrogen of the amide group.
reject: N-methyl means the methyl group attaches to the oxygen of the carbonyl.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the name of CH₃COCl?
records.back: Ethanoyl chloride.
accept: CH3COCl is called ethanoyl chloride.
reject: CH3COCl is named ethyl chloride.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the name of (CH₃CO)₂O?
records.back: Ethanoic anhydride.
accept: (CH3CO)2O is ethanoic anhydride.
reject: (CH3CO)2O is ethanoyl chloride.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the name of CH₃CONH₂?
records.back: Ethanamide.
accept: CH3CONH2 is called ethanamide.
reject: CH3CONH2 is ethylamine.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Which functional group in salicylic acid becomes an ester in aspirin?
records.back: The phenolic O–H group.
accept: Aspirin formation esterifies the phenol hydroxyl on salicylic acid.
reject: In making aspirin the carboxylic acid group is converted into a primary amide.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What organic by-product is associated with aspirin made using ethanoic anhydride?
records.back: Ethanoic acid.
accept: The side product of making aspirin with ethanoic anhydride is ethanoic acid.
reject: Aspirin synthesis using ethanoic anhydride releases HCl.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How is the limiting reagent identified?
records.back: Compare moles available divided by their balanced-equation coefficients.
accept: Divide each available amount in moles by its coefficient in the balanced equation and choose the smallest.
reject: The reactant with the smallest mass in grams must be limiting.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why must a limiting-reagent calculation consider stoichiometry?
records.back: Equal numbers of moles do not imply reactants are present in required ratios.
accept: The chemical equation coefficients determine the required mole ratios, so simply comparing mole counts is insufficient.
reject: Stoichiometric coefficients can be ignored when identifying which reagent is limiting.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Write the net ionic equation for acid–alkali neutralisation.
records.back: H⁺(aq)+OH⁻(aq)→H₂O(l).
accept: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l).
reject: The net ionic equation for neutralisation is H+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> HCl(aq).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Why is completing the square useful for a quadratic?
records.back: It reveals the turning point and helps solve or sketch the quadratic.
accept: Completing the square exposes the vertex and makes solving or plotting a quadratic easier.
reject: Completing the square changes the roots and therefore creates a different quadratic.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does the discriminant tell you?
records.back: For ax²+bx+c, Δ=b²−4ac: >0 two real roots, =0 repeated root, <0 no real roots.
accept: Delta=b squared minus 4ac; positive means two real roots, zero a repeated root, negative no real roots.
reject: If the discriminant is negative a quadratic has two distinct real roots.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How does tan x relate to sin x and cos x?
records.back: tan x = sin x / cos x.
accept: Tangent is sin x over cos x.
reject: tan x equals cos x divided by sin x.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does a counterexample establish?
records.back: A universal statement is false.
accept: One counterexample is sufficient to refute a universal assertion.
reject: One example that supports a statement proves it for every real number.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the sum to infinity for a convergent geometric series?
records.back: S∞ = a/(1−r), valid when |r| < 1.
accept: For absolute value of r below one, S infinity equals a over one minus r.
reject: The sum to infinity formula is valid for every common ratio greater than one.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does a zero discriminant tell you about a quadratic?
records.back: It has one repeated real root.
accept: There is a repeated real solution when the discriminant is zero.
reject: Zero discriminant means no real solutions.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does Σ from r=1 to n mean?
records.back: Add the listed expression for r = 1, 2, …, n.
accept: Summation from r=1 to n adds terms for each integer r from one through n.
reject: Sigma from 1 to n means multiply each of the terms.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For a geometric sum, what happens when r=1?
records.back: All n terms equal a, so Sₙ = na.
accept: When r=1 every term is a, making the sum n times a.
reject: With ratio one, the geometric sum is a/(1-1).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does f′(a)=0 tell you about a smooth curve?
records.back: It has a stationary point at x=a.
accept: At x=a the curve has zero gradient and so is stationary.
reject: The equation f'(a)=0 always means f(a)=0.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Why is the constant of integration needed in an indefinite integral?
records.back: All antiderivatives differ by a constant.
accept: Indefinite integration gives a family of antiderivatives differing by a constant.
reject: The constant can be omitted because all indefinite integrals have a unique antiderivative.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For a>1, what does y = af(x) do to y = f(x)?
records.back: A vertical stretch by scale factor a.
accept: Multiplying f(x) by a stretches vertically by scale factor a.
reject: The transformation y=af(x) stretches horizontally by factor a.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For a positive integer n, what does n! mean?
accept: n factorial is the product of all positive integers from one to n.
reject: n! means n plus (n-1) plus all earlier positive integers.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the factorial of zero (0!)?
accept: Zero factorial is equal to one.
reject: 0! equals zero.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: In the recurrence uₙ₊₁ = f(uₙ), how is the next term found?
records.back: Substitute the previous term uₙ into f.
accept: Find the next term by evaluating f at the preceding term.
reject: The next term always equals the previous term plus one.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: When is a sequence strictly increasing?
records.back: When every term is greater than the previous one.
accept: Every consecutive difference u_(n+1)-u_n must be positive.
reject: Strictly increasing means successive terms are allowed to be equal.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For an upward-opening quadratic with two distinct roots, where is f(x)>0?
records.back: Outside the roots.
accept: For an upward parabola with two distinct real roots, positive f(x) lies left of the smaller root and right of the larger.
reject: An upward quadratic is positive only between its two real roots.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What happens to an inequality sign when multiplying by a negative number?
records.back: Reverse the inequality sign.
accept: Reverse the direction of the inequality whenever multiplying both sides by a negative.
reject: Multiplying both sides of an inequality by minus one keeps the inequality direction unchanged.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does a perpendicular from a circle's centre to a chord do?
records.back: It bisects the chord.
accept: A line from the centre perpendicular to a chord divides that chord into two equal lengths.
reject: The perpendicular from a circle's centre divides the chord into unequal lengths.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the angle in a semicircle, subtended by its diameter?
accept: The angle opposite a diameter on a circle is a right angle.
reject: The angle in a semicircle is always 180 degrees.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the exact value of sin 30°?
accept: sin of thirty degrees equals one half.
reject: sin 30 degrees equals square root three over two.
